children.value: Learning Rate and Stability
How does learning rate affect the training of a small CNN?
Imagine teaching a computer to recognize different types of clothing. At first, it won’t recognize everything correctly. It makes mistakes, learns from them, and tries to make better predictions.
But here’s something worth thinking about: how much should the computer adjust each time it makes a mistake?

This is where the learning rate comes in. It controls how big or small the adjustments are while the model is learning. If the adjustments are too small, learning may take longer. But if they are too big, the model might struggle to learn properly.
So, how does the learning rate affect the way a model learns? And what happens when the learning rate is too high?
To find out, five different learning rates were tested using the Fashion-MNIST dataset and a small CNN.
1. Understanding Learning Rate
Before looking at the experiment, let’s first understand what happens when a neural network learns.
A neural network has values called weights and biases. These values help the model recognize patterns and make predictions. During training, the model adjusts these values to improve its predictions.

Think of it like walking toward a destination. If your steps are too small, it will take longer to get there. But if your steps are too big, you might go past your destination. Learning rate works in a similar way. It controls how big each adjustment is.
During training, the model follows a few steps:
It makes a prediction.
It checks how wrong the prediction is using a loss function.
It calculates a gradient to determine how the model’s values should change.
It updates its weights and biases to improve its next predict
A simplified formula for updating a weight is:
w_{\text{new}} = w_{\text{old}} - \alpha \times \text{gradient}

For this experiment, Adam was used as the optimizer. Think of an optimizer as the method that helps update the model’s weights and biases. Adam uses information from current and previous gradients to guide these updates, while the learning rate controls their overall size.

But how can you tell if the model is learning properly? One way is to look at its loss during training. When the loss goes down over time, it is usually a good sign. If it keeps increasing or changing sharply, the model may be having difficulty learning.
2. Experiment Setup
Now that the learning rate is clearer, let’s see how it was tested.
The experiment used Fashion-MNIST, a dataset containing grayscale images of clothing. Each image is 28 × 28 pixels and belongs to one of 10 clothing categories.
A small Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was used to classify these images. CNNs are useful for image tasks because they can recognize patterns such as shapes, edges, and other visual features.
To see what happens when the learning rate changes, five different values were tested:
Run
Learning rate
Only the learning rate was changed. All the other settings stayed the same to make the comparison fair.

Now comes the interesting part: what actually happened after running the experiments?

Looking at the table, the learning rate of 0.001 had the lowest average validation loss and the highest average validation accuracy. The 0.0001 setting also performed well, while 0.1 showed the most inconsistent results.

This graph makes it easier to compare the final validation loss of all five learning rates. Remember, a lower validation loss means the model made fewer errors on the validation images.
The 0.001 learning rate had the lowest average validation loss, followed by 0.0001. On the other hand, 0.1 had the highest average loss and the biggest difference between its three runs.
4. What Do the Results Tell Us?

children.label: 4. What Do the Results Tell Us?

children.value: After looking at the table and graphs, one thing becomes clear: the learning rate can make a big difference in how a model learns.

The smallest learning rate, 0.00001, still improved during training. However, it reached only 78.30% average validation accuracy. This suggests that its adjustments were too small to reach the same performance as the better-performing settings within four epochs.

The 0.0001 and 0.001 learning rates gave the best results. Among the five values, 0.001 performed the best, reaching 88.47% average validation accuracy and 0.3148 average validation loss. Its results were also fairly consistent across the three runs.
The 0.01 learning rate also learned, but its average validation accuracy was lower at 84.98%. Its results also varied more than those of 0.0001 and 0.001.
Now, let’s look at the largest learning rate: 0.1.
Two of its three runs ended with validation accuracy close to 10%, while the third reached 73.13%. Since Fashion-MNIST has 10 categories, an accuracy close to 10% is similar to guessing.

However, none of the runs produced non-finite loss values such as NaN. This means it would not be accurate to say that all three runs completely failed. Instead, the results show that 0.1 was unreliable for this particular experiment.

So, what does all of this tell us? A learning rate that is too small can slow down learning, while one that is too large can make training inconsistent. Finding a suitable value is important for getting better and more stable results.
Limitations
Of course, there are a few things to keep in mind when looking at these results.

Only 10,000 training images and 6,000 validation images were used instead of the full dataset. The model was also trained for only four epochs, so the results might have been different with more training time.

The experiment also used only one CNN architecture and the Adam optimizer. Other models or optimizers may produce different results. Although three random seeds were tested, they are still not enough to make strong statistical claims.
Because of these limitations, the results only show what happened with this particular setup. They do not mean that 0.001 will always be the best learning rate for every CNN.
5. Key Takeaways
After going through the experiment, here are three things worth remembering:
Learning rate matters. It controls how big the model’s adjustments are during training, which affects how quickly it learns.
A bigger learning rate is not always better. In this experiment, 0.1 produced inconsistent results, while 0.001 gave the best average validation performance.

One run may not tell the whole story. Testing different random seeds helped show that the same learning rate can produce different results. Comparing multiple runs gives a better picture of how the model performs.
